Ruth Vance walks into Harrow Bench at dusk with a stoppered jar of seed, and the valley's oldest rule takes over before anyone asks her name: she is fed at the first house she reaches, given three nights in an aired bed, and told that on the fourth morning a meeting will decide whether she stays. It is a fair rule, and an old wound. The last stranger who ate at this table left with a jar of Harrow Bench's own seed and never sent it back, which is why Martha Gale, who holds one of the two keys to the seed store, has not signed for anyone since. Tom Leary, born the spring after the quiet ended and the only person in the valley anyone is allowed to ask about it, finds a short unentered row growing where his water runs — against the rule that says an unentered row is pulled up by whoever finds it. He does not pull it up. What grows in that row, what is actually in Ruth's jar, and whether Martha will put her name beside a stranger's again come due on Sunday morning, when the meeting has to decide not who is right, but what this place is for. A small, patient novel about a village, a well, a ledger, and the slow work of deciding who gets to stay.

For readers of *A Gentle Creature* and *Station Eleven*, and viewers of *Local Hero*.
# Chapter 1 — Fed at the First House

The bridge was stone and the road past it was not mended, and Ruth Vance came off it into woodsmoke at dusk.

The first house had a lamp in the window and a pot already on. A woman opened the door before she knocked, looked at her boots and not her face, and said, "Sit down, it's nearly ready."

So she sat. Bread, a cut apple, a cup of well water so cold it made her teeth ache. Nobody asked her name. She set the jar on the table beside her plate, stoppered, and left her hand near it. A young man at the hearth — eighteen or so, sleeves pushed up, wet to the elbow from something — looked at the jar, and looked at it again, and said nothing about it.

A man came in without knocking while she was still eating.

"Owen Pike," he said, to the room. "I've aired you a bed at the inn. Don't argue, it was aired anyway." He pulled out a chair and turned it round and sat on it backwards. "Three nights. That's the rule, that's not me. Thursday, Friday, Saturday, and Sunday morning the meeting decides whether you stay. There's no money here. There's a ledger, and the ledger is the money — names, rows, debts of work. I'd like yours in it by Sunday."

"You don't know anything about me," Ruth said.

"No," Owen agreed, pleased. "That's Sunday's problem."

She finished the apple. Then she asked the thing she had carried up the road all afternoon. "The flats above the upper well. Are they spoken for?"

The young man at the hearth answered. "The pipe runs without carrying," he said. "You don't haul to the flats. That's why anything grown for trade goes there." He dried his hands. "Tom Leary. You can ask me things."

"Why you?"

"Born the spring after. I only know what I was told."

The door opened again and a woman stood in it, not coming through. Grey hair, coat still buttoned.

"Martha Gale," she said. "Seed store's in the vestry. It opens after the meeting, never before, and never by one person — two names in the room, both sign." She said it the way you'd say the well was forty feet. "I'm not saying no to you."

"You're not saying yes."

"I haven't signed for a stranger since last autumn," Martha said, and left it there on the step, and went.

Afterwards Ruth stood in the yard with the jar in both hands, turning it slowly, feeling the seed shift inside. Above the roofline the flats lay dark and level against a darker hill.

Three nights.

She put the jar in her coat and went in to sleep.
# Chapter 2 — What the Pipe Turned Up

The frost had got into the pipe collar, and Tom Leary worked it loose with his thumbs because a tool would have cracked it. Six years of this. The blockage came out as a wad of leaf mould and one flat stone he could not account for, and then the water went through with a knock he felt in the wood of the trough.

He followed the wet line down because his boots always did.

The row was in the good corner of the flats. Eight feet, nine. Drilled straight, the soil firmed along it with the side of a boot, and dark all down its length where somebody had carried water to it from his pipe. Not a mark in the ledger anywhere with that row against it.

He crouched at the end of it. An unentered row is pulled up by whoever finds it. He had known the sentence since he could read. He put his hands on his knees and left them there.

Ruth Vance came up the path with an empty can, not hurrying.

"I don't apologise for it," she said. "A row you can see is an argument. A jar is only a promise."

"What's in it?"

"Skirret." She set the can down. "You had it here. It went out of the valley — before me, before you. I've enough for one row and nothing over."

He had never seen it grow. He had only been told about it, which was how he knew everything that came from before.

An hour later he stood on Martha Gale's step with his boots still wet and asked her why she had stopped signing.

She did not ask why he wanted to know. "Last autumn's walker," she said. "We fed him, entered him, gave him a bed and a row. He wintered well. He went out in spring with a jar of Harrow seed and the jar has not come back." She looked past him at the frost going off the wall. "I've held the walnut ground since. Part of that's grief and part of it's spite and I can't always tell you which is which on a given morning."

It was the longest she had spoken to him in a year.

He walked home past the flats in the full light. The row was still standing, greenless, a line of firmed earth in the corner where the water ran best. He had not pulled it up. He had not told anyone. By tomorrow's dawn both of those would be things he had to say out loud, in the chapel, in front of everybody.

So he began, slowly, working out what he would ask for in return.
# Chapter 3 — Sunday, Two Names

The meeting began with a slate. It had come off the inn roof in the week's wind, and Owen Pike wanted two hands on Tuesday to put it back, and got them before he finished asking. Then the bridge road, which was clear. Then somebody's dog and somebody's hens, settled the way such things settle, with nobody much minding.

Martha Gale sat on the cold end of the second bench and waited. Behind her the vestry door was shut, and through the wall the ledger lay open on the table where it always lay.

Owen made his case warmly, which was his fault and his use. Three nights. Fed at the Learys'. No trouble, no taking. A valley nobody arrives in, he said, has agreed to end.

"A tree planted for a stranger," Martha said, "is a tree we don't eat from. I'm not signing." She said it without heat. She had said it before.

Tom Leary stood up.

"I found a row on the flats yesterday at dawn," he said. "Unentered. Watered off my pipe. The rule says I pull it up." He looked at the window. "I didn't."

Nobody spoke.

"I'm not asking to be forgiven. I want my own line in the ledger. My name, not my mother's."

Ruth Vance said her piece short. Skirret, she said. The valley grew it once and stopped. Enough in the jar for one row, and the jar goes to the store whether the row is hers or not. Then she sat down. The argument was standing on the flats, and anyone could walk up and look at it.

Martha went into the vestry, because that was where she thought. Walnut ground in her head, laid out as she had held it since last autumn. Shelves she had not opened for a stranger in a year. She had been keeping ground for a boy who would never get a line while she kept it.

She came back and said she would sign, and that the second name should be Tom's.

So the store was opened by two names, both signing, as the rule required and always had. Ruth's name went into the ledger beside the row already in the ground. The jar went onto the shelf, labelled in Martha's hand, small letters, the date under it.

"The walnut ground stays walnut," Martha said, and nobody argued.

Then people went out to do ordinary things with their hands. Tom walked up to clear the pipe that watered a row with his own name at the top of it. Down on the flats the short line of firmed earth lay waiting, and the valley was not particularly watching.
